title: Ἀλώπεκες ⟨ἐπὶ τῷ Μαιάνδρῳ⟩
part: The Foxes at the Maeander (Chambry 29 · Perry 232)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 29 (= Perry 232). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ποτὲ ἀλώπεκες ἐπὶ τὸν Μαίανδρον ποταμὸν συνηθροίσθησαν, πιεῖν ἐξ αὐτοῦ θέλουσαι.
sentences.tr: Pote alōpekes epi ton Maiandron potamon synēthroisthēsan, piein ex autou thelousai.
sentences.l: Once foxes gathered together at the river Maeander, wishing to drink from it.
sentences.n: The Maeander is the great winding river of Caria, in Asia Minor; its bends gave English the verb 'to meander'. In the title Chambry prints ⟨ἐπὶ τῷ Μαιάνδρῳ⟩ inside angle brackets: those are his mark for words he has supplied himself, not words carried by the manuscripts.

sentences.t: Διὰ δὲ τὸ ῥοιζηδὸν φέρεσθαι τὸ ὕδωρ, ἀλλήλας προτρεπόμεναι οὐκ ἐτόλμων εἰσελθεῖν.
sentences.tr: Dia de to rhoizēdon pheresthai to hydōr, allēlas protrepomenai ouk etolmōn eiselthein.
sentences.l: But on account of the water's rushing along with a roar, urging one another on, they did not dare to go in.
sentences.i: But because the water swept past with a roar, they kept urging one another forward and none of them dared to go in.
sentences.n: διὰ τό + infinitive is the articular infinitive giving a cause — literally 'on account of the to-be-carried of the water' — where English says 'because the water rushed'. It is one of Greek's commonest ways of packing a clause into a phrase. ῥοιζηδόν is a rare adverb from ῥοῖζος, the whistling rush of an arrow. The imperfect ἐτόλμων holds them at the bank, hesitating on and on.

sentences.t: Μιᾶς δὲ αὐτῶν διεξιούσης, ἐπὶ τῷ εὐτελίζειν τὰς λοιπὰς καὶ δειλίαν καταγελώσης, ἑαυτὴν ὡς γενναιοτέραν προκρίνασα θαρσαλέως εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ ἐπήδησεν.
sentences.tr: Mias de autōn diexiousēs, epi tōi eutelizein tas loipas kai deilian katagelōsēs, heautēn hōs gennaioteran prokrinasa tharsaleōs eis to hydōr epēdēsen.
sentences.l: But one of them coming forward, so as to belittle the rest, and laughing at their cowardice, having preferred herself as braver, boldly leapt into the water.
sentences.i: Then one of them pushed forward, running the others down and laughing at their cowardice; rating herself the braver, she leapt boldly into the water.
sentences.n: The sentence changes construction in mid-course: it begins as a genitive absolute (Μιᾶς … διεξιούσης … καταγελώσης) and then finishes with a nominative participle and a finite verb (προκρίνασα … ἐπήδησεν), as though the fox had been the subject all along. Such slips are common in the fable collections and are left as printed. δειλίαν as a direct object of καταγελάω is also loose — that verb normally takes the genitive of the person laughed at — so 'laughing at their cowardice' is the sense rather than a tidy construction. διεξιούσης is not certain: διέξειμι 'go out through' would make it pushing her way to the front, but the same verb commonly means 'go through in words, hold forth', which would suit a fox making a speech at the others.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ῥεύματος ταύτην εἰς μέσον κατασύραντος, καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν παρὰ τὴν ὄχθην τοῦ ποταμοῦ ἑστηκυιῶν, πρὸς αὐτὴν εἰπουσῶν· « Μὴ ἐάσῃς ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ στραφεῖσα ὑπόδειξον τὴν εἴσοδον δι’ ἧς ἀκινδύνως δυνησόμεθα πιεῖν, » ἐκείνη ἀπαγομένη ἔλεγεν· « Ἀπόκρισιν ἔχω εἰς Μίλητον, καὶ ταύτην ἐκεῖσε ἀποκομίσαι βούλομαι· ἐν δὲ τῷ ἐπανιέναι με ὑποδείξω ὑμῖν. »
sentences.tr: Tou de rheumatos tautēn eis meson katasyrantos, kai tōn loipōn para tēn ochthēn tou potamou hestēkuiōn, pros autēn eipousōn· « Mē easēis hēmas, alla strapheisa hypodeixon tēn eisodon di’ hēs akindynōs dynēsometha piein, » ekeinē apagomenē elegen· « Apokrisin echō eis Milēton, kai tautēn ekeise apokomisai boulomai· en de tōi epanienai me hypodeixō hymin. »
sentences.l: But the current having dragged her into the middle, and the rest standing on the bank of the river and saying to her: « Do not leave us, but turn round and point out the way in through which we shall be able to drink without danger, » she, being carried off, kept saying: « I have an answer for Miletus, and I want to carry it there; and on my way back I will point it out to you. »
sentences.i: The current dragged her out into midstream, and the others, standing on the bank, called to her: « Don't abandon us — turn back and show us the way in where we can drink safely. » And she, as she was swept away, kept saying: « I have a message for Miletus, and I mean to get it there; I will show you on my way back. »
sentences.n: Three genitive absolutes run one after another (τοῦ ῥεύματος … κατασύραντος, τῶν λοιπῶν … ἑστηκυιῶν, εἰπουσῶν) before the main clause finally arrives at ἐκείνη … ἔλεγεν. Μὴ ἐάσῃς is the regular prohibition, μή with the aorist subjunctive rather than an imperative. ἐν δὲ τῷ ἐπανιέναι με is another articular infinitive, this time with its own accusative subject: 'in my coming back'. The joke rests on geography: the Maeander empties into the sea at Miletus, so the current is already carrying her there — she is drowning, and answers as though she were on an errand.

sentences.t: Πρὸς τοὺς κατὰ ἀλαζονείαν ἑαυτοῖς κίνδυνον ἐπιφέροντας.
sentences.tr: Pros tous kata alazoneian heautois kindynon epipherontas.
sentences.l: Against those who out of boastfulness bring danger upon themselves.
sentences.n: A moral with no verb at all: just πρός with the accusative, 'aimed at…'. Elsewhere the collection fills the frame out — ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος, 'the story is well timed' — and here it is simply left to be understood. ἀλαζονεία is the swagger of the ἀλαζών, the braggart of Greek comedy.
